reasoning: The strongest post so far is a human body reel with a 'what happens to your body' hook. 'Without sleep' reached 103 accounts and earned the page's first 2 shares. Psychology reels came second (30 reach). Fear combines both categories, is evergreen and is easy to relate to. That stays inside the niche, in line with the plan to cut news. I'm keeping the reel format and 5 slides. Each slide states the claim directly, for the hook test. The music is mystery to suit the topic. Palette 4 continues the rotation, since it has barely been tested. The caption question asks for a personal story to test whether that drives comments.
topic: Fear response: amygdala, adrenaline, digestion, goosebumps, time slowing
hook: What fear does to your body in seconds

slides.title: Your brain reacts first
slides.body: Your amygdala flags danger before the thinking part of your brain even knows what it saw.
slides.image_prompt: A dark forest path at night with glowing red warning light deep between the trees, eerie fog, cinematic
slides.credit: Brenda Clarke from Blaxland, Australia (CC BY 2.0) via wikimedia

slides.title: Adrenaline floods in
slides.body: Adrenaline makes your heart pound and your breathing speed up, sending extra oxygen to your muscles.
slides.image_prompt: A glowing anatomical heart surrounded by electric sparks and rushing red light streams, dark background

slides.title: Your gut shuts down
slides.body: Blood is pulled away from your stomach, which is why fear feels like butterflies or nausea.
slides.image_prompt: Dozens of dark moths fluttering inside a glass jar on a shadowy table, dramatic side lighting
slides.credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, K. Noll, J. Kastner, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb) (CC BY 4.0) via wikimedia

slides.title: Goosebumps appear
slides.body: Tiny muscles raise your hairs, a leftover reflex that once made furry ancestors look bigger.
slides.image_prompt: Close-up of a frightened black cat with its fur standing on end, arched back, moody lighting

slides.title: Time seems to slow
slides.body: Fear makes your brain store denser memories, so scary moments feel longer when you remember them.
slides.image_prompt: An hourglass with sand frozen mid-fall, floating grains suspended in the air, dark dramatic background

cta: Follow so you never miss the next one
caption:
Fear hits your body before you even know what scared you. Your amygdala sounds the alarm first, and adrenaline handles the rest in seconds.

One strange bonus: in a 2007 experiment, people who free-fell 31 metres into a net felt the drop lasted about a third longer than it did. Their brains weren't slowing time. They were just recording more memory.

What's a scary moment you still remember in slow motion?
